stem: Which interpretation matches the ecosystem and cross-platform cards as course feature descriptions, rather than a current inventory or universal compatibility certificate?

options.text: Ecosystem counts certify every package on every host; cross-platform guarantees identical drivers on those hosts
Ecosystem means every package is maintained by the core ROS team; cross-platform means the same compiled executable runs unchanged on every host
Ecosystem refers only to packages shipped inside the core installation; cross-platform means those packages need no platform-specific dependencies
Ecosystem highlights reusable packages and users; cross-platform names Linux, macOS and Windows as ROS 2 hosts

citations.locator: Lecture 5, printed slide 4; Printed 4. Definition and four cards: open source with BSD/Apache-2.0/community wording; middleware abstraction; ecosystem counts of 1000+ packages and 10000+ users; ROS 2 support for Linux, macOS and Windows. Counts are source claims, not current measurements.

stem: In the course’s get_map example, which request/response directions and client arrangement match its intended service model?

options.text: Nav broadcasts OccupancyGrid to Map; Map returns get_map to Nav; the clients act as the intended map servers
Nav sends get_map to Map; Map returns OccupancyGrid to Nav; several clients may call that intended Map service server
Map sends get_map to Nav; Nav returns OccupancyGrid to Map; several clients may call that intended Nav service server
Nav sends get_map to Map; Map returns OccupancyGrid to Nav; the service is restricted to one client for its lifetime

assumptions: Use the intended single named server in this course example; this is not an assertion that middleware enforces global uniqueness of server names.

citations.locator: Lecture 5, physical PDF page 194: service prose, including the intended multiple-client arrangement; not the diagram on page 195

Lecture 5, printed slide 25; Printed 25. Untitled diagram: Nav Node client on the left sends get_map() to Map Node server on the right. A reverse arrow returns OccupancyGrid. Both arrow directions were visually inspected.

stem: Consider a hypothetical single non-preemptive motor loop: the next PWM update is due at t=1 ms, but a synchronous CNN call runs from t=0 to t=8 ms before the loop can service it. With no other delay or hardware offload, how late is that first update?

options.text: 0 ms late
1 ms late
8 ms late
7 ms late

assumptions: The numerical timings are hypothetical givens, not measurements reported by the lecture.
The loop is single-threaded and non-preemptive, the CNN call blocks until t=8 ms, and no separate PWM hardware or task services the deadline.
Evaluate the first pending update only; ignore all other delays.

citations.locator: Lecture 5, printed slide 11; Printed 11. The course uses a Jetson Orin Nano host for GPU-assisted vision and middleware coordination, alongside a simpler Arduino motor-control role. Centralization is the example architecture, not a universal requirement.

Lecture 5, printed slide 30; Printed 30. Depth camera/LiDAR input, with USB/CSI examples, is published through sensor drivers. GPU perception subscribes and detects; decision logic selects movement. Connection examples are not universal for every sensor.

Lecture 5, printed slide 31; Printed 31. Chain: 3D camera; sensor_msgs/Image; Jetson ROS/Python AI/GPU; serial-data/PWM label; Arduino/motor shield; H-bridge; DC motors; physical motion. Body assigns precise PWM timing to the low-level microcontroller, not to CNN inference.

stem: In a hypothetical URDF link, a visible fin is centered at x=+0.15 m, while the existing collision box spans x=−0.10 to +0.10 m; which change models fin contacts at the correct location while retaining the existing body collision and visual geometry?

options.text: Move the existing body collision box center to x=+0.15 m instead of retaining it and adding the fin
Keep collision geometry unchanged and increase only the fin’s contribution to the inertial mass
Keep the body collision box and add a fin collision shape with its link-frame center at x=+0.15 m
Keep the body collision box and add the same fin collision shape with its link-frame center at x=−0.15 m

assumptions: The dimensions are hypothetical and refer to one common link frame; other axes and fin dimensions are chosen correctly.
The task is model-geometry correction, not proof of numerical contact accuracy or physical validation.

citations.locator: Lecture 5, printed slide 32; Printed 32. URDF is XML for appearance, dimensions and kinematic structure. Rigid links have visual, collision and inertial properties. Joint examples are fixed camera mount, continuous wheel and revolute arm hinge. A model property alone is not a safety certificate.

Lecture 5, printed slide 35; Printed 35. Sim-to-real uses middleware abstraction and common interfaces to reuse robot computation. Gazebo supplies simulated physical effects; RViz visualizes robot data. Minimal code changes is a design aim, not proof of identical real-world behavior.

Lecture 5, printed slide 38; Printed 38. Gazebo cards cover rigid-body physics and collisions, simulated cameras/LiDAR/IMU/GPS, bidirectional ros_gz topic bridging, SDF worlds/models, Ignition-to-Gz naming, and hardware-in-the-loop. Engine and release names are version-dependent examples rather than current installation guidance; bridge configuration matters for ROS messages.

stem: Which experiment most directly matches hardware-in-the-loop rather than an entirely simulated, entirely physical or playback-only setup?

options.text: A physical controller exchanges live signals with a Gazebo-simulated plant, and RViz displays the resulting data
A simulated controller exchanges live signals with a Gazebo-simulated plant, and RViz displays the resulting data
A physical controller operates a physical plant, and RViz displays the resulting data
RViz displays recorded sensor messages while neither a controller nor a simulated plant is actively coupled

assumptions: Classify only the components explicitly described in each option; no additional hardware or simulation is implied.

citations.locator: Lecture 5, printed slide 35; Printed 35. Sim-to-real uses middleware abstraction and common interfaces to reuse robot computation.
